internship.title: MERN Stack Web Development Internship
internship.description: An industry-oriented internship that takes an intern from reproducible setup and Git workflow through React interface engineering, Node.js/Express API work, MongoDB/Mongoose data modeling, authentication and authorization, client/server integration, testing, security, performance, professional review, and release preparation. The program is organized around progressively realistic engineering work, not just a sequence of lessons, and culminates in one substantial Team Task Board capstone.
prerequisites: Basic JavaScript syntax, functions, arrays, objects, and modules.
Basic HTML/CSS including forms and semantic elements.
objectives: Build and explain a complete MERN application from requirements.
Work with branches, commits, reviewable changes, and merge conflicts.
Build accessible React interfaces with state, forms, routing, and asynchronous data.
Design Express APIs with validation, status codes, and safe error handling.
Model MongoDB data with Mongoose schemas, indexes, pagination, and query-aware patterns.
Implement password hashing, JWT authentication, role checks, and object-level authorization.
Write unit, API, and browser-level tests around critical behavior.
Review web security, dependency risk, performance questions, and release configuration.
Document setup, architecture, troubleshooting, and release readiness.

competencies.name: Engineering workflow
competencies.description: Breaks requirements into small, verifiable changes and uses Git for collaborative work.

competencies.name: React implementation
competencies.description: Builds stateful, accessible, responsive interfaces with clear component boundaries.

competencies.name: API engineering
competencies.description: Builds predictable Express endpoints with validation, authorization, and safe errors.

competencies.name: Data engineering
competencies.description: Models MongoDB data and selects indexes from query patterns.

competencies.name: Identity and access control
competencies.description: Protects credentials and enforces server-side authorization.

competencies.name: Testing
competencies.description: Chooses suitable test levels and creates durable regression coverage.

competencies.name: Security mindset
competencies.description: Treats inputs, dependencies, secrets, configuration, and logs as security boundaries.

competencies.name: Performance reasoning
competencies.description: Measures before optimizing and uses evidence from query plans and client tooling.

competencies.name: Technical communication
competencies.description: Documents architecture, decisions, risks, and verification evidence.

modules.title: Onboarding and Engineering Workflow
modules.description: Establish the habits and repository practices expected of an intern working on a shared MERN codebase.
objectives: Work with focused branches and commits.
Turn requirements into verifiable acceptance criteria.

lessons.title: MERN as a Request-Response System
lessons.description: Trace how a browser action becomes an HTTP request, reaches an Express handler, crosses a data layer, and returns JSON to React.
learningObjectives: explain the roles of React, Node.js, Express, MongoDB, and Mongoose
notes: MERN names technologies with distinct responsibilities rather than one monolithic framework. React owns UI composition; Node provides the runtime; Express handles HTTP concerns; MongoDB persists documents; Mongoose provides application-level schema/model abstractions.
lessons.summary: A strong intern can explain the system as cooperating layers and identify the server as the authority for protected operations.

lessons.title: Local Toolchain and Reproducibility
lessons.description: Set up current supported Node/Vite tooling, understand package metadata, and make the project easy for another developer to reproduce.
learningObjectives: explain package.json scripts and dependency roles
notes: Node.js production guidance recommends Active LTS or Maintenance LTS releases. The researched environment lists Node 24 as LTS. Vite current guidance requires Node 20.19+ or 22.12+ depending on the line/template.
lessons.summary: The project should be installable and understandable without relying on a developer-specific machine setup.

lessons.title: Git Branches, Commits, and Merge Conflicts
lessons.description: Use Git as an engineering tool for isolating work, reviewing changes, and recovering from integration problems.
notes: Small commits make review and rollback easier. A merge conflict is not an error in Git; it is a signal that competing edits need a human decision.
lessons.summary: The intern can work in a branch, inspect a diff, resolve a conflict, and leave a clean history.

practicals.title: Resolve a Feature-Branch Conflict
practicals.description: Practice the repository workflow expected in a collaborative internship. The exercise deliberately creates a small documentation conflict so the intern experiences conflict inspection, resolution, and verification.
steps: Create a repository with a main branch.
Create a feature/task-filter branch and make one focused documentation change.
Create another branch that changes the same line.
Merge the second branch into main and inspect the conflict markers.
Resolve the conflict using the intended final wording.
Commit the resolution and inspect the graph.
practicals.solution:
git switch -c feature/task-filter
# edit README.md in the feature branch

git add README.md
git commit -m "Document task filtering"

git switch main
git switch -c feature/assignee-filter
# edit the same README line differently

git add README.md
git commit -m "Document assignee filtering"

git switch main
git merge feature/assignee-filter

# Resolve the conflict in README.md, then:
git add README.md
git commit -m "Resolve documentation merge conflict"
git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all
practicals.output: A clean working tree with an explicit conflict-resolution commit and a history that shows both feature branches.

quiz.question: Which Git command creates and switches to a new branch?
quiz.explanation: It creates a new branch from the current commit and switches the working tree to it.

lessons.title: Requirements, Acceptance Criteria, and Documentation
lessons.description: Turn an ambiguous feature request into bounded engineering work and document assumptions for the rest of the team.
notes: A requirement says what behavior is needed; an implementation choice says how it is achieved. Acceptance criteria should be observable enough that a test or reviewer can verify them.
lessons.summary: A useful issue or ticket makes it clear what to build and how success will be verified.

modules.assessment: Demonstrate a clean feature branch, meaningful commits, and a reproducible setup description.

modules.title: React Interface Engineering
modules.description: Build maintainable, stateful React interfaces with accessible forms, routing, effects, and asynchronous data flows.
objectives: Manage state and derived data correctly.
Create accessible and resilient UI states.

lessons.title: Components and Composition
lessons.description: Design React components around clear responsibilities and compose them into pages.
notes: React components are JavaScript functions that return markup. Composition allows a parent to own orchestration while smaller children remain focused.
lessons.summary: The intern can create a page from understandable component boundaries.

lessons.title: State, Events, and Derived Data
lessons.description: Use state for changing information and derive views instead of duplicating state.
learningObjectives: derive filtered data from source state
notes: Duplicating a value in state creates synchronization risk. Store the source of truth and calculate derived views from it.
lessons.summary: The intern can choose what belongs in state and what should be computed.

lessons.title: Effects and External Synchronization
lessons.description: Use effects only when synchronizing with systems outside React and clean up asynchronous work when needed.
learningObjectives: avoid effect loops caused by derived state
notes: Effects are for synchronization with external systems such as network requests, timers, subscriptions, or browser APIs. Pure calculations normally belong in rendering or derived expressions.
lessons.summary: The intern can explain why an effect exists and what resource it synchronizes.

lessons.title: Forms, Validation, and Accessibility
lessons.description: Create labeled, keyboard-friendly forms with useful validation feedback while retaining server-side validation as authoritative.
learningObjectives: distinguish client UX validation from server validation
notes: Client validation improves UX; it is not a security boundary. Use native HTML semantics first, then add ARIA only where necessary.
lessons.summary: The intern can produce forms that are understandable with keyboard navigation and assistive technology.

lessons.title: Routing and Page Composition
lessons.description: Structure client-side navigation into route-level screens and reusable controls.
notes: Routing determines which page component is rendered for a location. Keep navigation concerns separate from domain logic so pages remain testable.
lessons.summary: Navigation structure mirrors the product’s information architecture.

lessons.title: Fetching Data and Handling Async UI States
lessons.description: Fetch API data and explicitly model loading, empty, error, and success states.
notes: A rejected network request and an HTTP 404 are different failure modes; fetch resolves for HTTP error statuses, so applications must inspect response.ok/status.
lessons.summary: The client behaves predictably when the network is slow, unavailable, or returns an error.

practicals.title: Build an Accessible Task Filter
practicals.description: Implement a controlled React filter with a labeled select, derived data, and an accessible empty state.
steps: Create task data with open, in-progress, and done states.
Store the selected status in state.
Add a label and select control.
Derive the visible list from the selected status without mutating source data.
Render an explicit empty state when there are no matches.
practicals.output: The select remains controlled by React state and the list changes without mutating the underlying task collection.

tasks.title: Build an Accessible Task Board Screen
tasks.description: Implement a responsive task board with labeled controls, filtering, empty states, and keyboard-visible focus.
tasks.problemStatement: Create a task board that filters by status and remains usable without a mouse.
constraints: Use native elements before adding ARIA.
tasks.hint: Start with semantic headings, labels, lists, and buttons before styling.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The component keeps the filter controlled, derives visible data, uses a label tied to the select, and communicates the dynamic list as a live region.

modules.assessment: Review the screen at desktop and narrow widths and demonstrate the keyboard path through its main controls.

modules.title: Node.js and Express API Engineering
modules.description: Implement HTTP APIs with clear contracts, middleware pipelines, validation, error handling, and testable business logic.
objectives: Separate transport logic from business rules.

lessons.title: Node.js Runtime and Async I/O
lessons.description: Understand the Node runtime at a practical level and avoid blocking the event loop with unnecessary synchronous work.
notes: Node is particularly effective for I/O-bound services. CPU-heavy synchronous work inside request handlers can block other requests.
lessons.summary: The intern can reason about why asynchronous database and network calls fit API servers.

lessons.title: Express Routing and Middleware
lessons.description: Build an Express pipeline where middleware order has intentional meaning.
notes: Express middleware functions can read or modify request/response state and either end the response or call next(). Ordering matters because later handlers see the state established by earlier middleware.
lessons.summary: The intern can explain the request pipeline from parsing through route logic to error handling.

lessons.title: HTTP Contracts and Status Codes
lessons.description: Define API behavior using methods, paths, query parameters, request bodies, status codes, and consistent JSON shapes.
notes: Status codes are part of the API contract. List endpoints should not accept arbitrary page sizes or arbitrary sort fields.
lessons.summary: The intern can describe an endpoint contract before coding it.

lessons.title: Boundary Validation and Safe Errors
lessons.description: Validate client-controlled data and centralize unexpected server errors.
learningObjectives: keep stack traces out of normal responses
notes: Validation belongs at trust boundaries. Unexpected errors should be logged server-side and represented to clients by stable, non-sensitive messages.
lessons.summary: The API has predictable validation failures and a safe error boundary.

practicals.title: Build a Validated Express Endpoint
practicals.description: Build a small Express API slice with boundary validation, meaningful status codes, and centralized unexpected-error handling.
steps: Create an Express app with JSON parsing.
Implement POST /api/tasks with title and priority validation.
Return 400 for invalid input and 201 for success.
Keep a small in-memory collection for the exercise.
Add GET /api/tasks.
Add an error middleware at the end of the pipeline.
practicals.output: Valid requests create tasks with 201; invalid input produces 400; unexpected errors do not expose stack traces to clients.

lessons.title: Service Boundaries and Testable Logic
lessons.description: Refactor domain decisions out of large route handlers so they can be tested independently.
learningObjectives: separate HTTP concerns from domain rules
notes: A route can coordinate parsing and response formatting while a service decides whether a user is allowed to rename a task, how validation applies, or how a state transition works.
lessons.summary: The intern can make business rules independently testable.

tasks.title: Refactor a Fat Route into a Service
tasks.description: Separate validation, authorization, and persistence decisions from an HTTP route.
tasks.problemStatement: A PATCH endpoint currently mixes parsing, ownership checks, persistence, and response formatting. Refactor it without changing its external contract.
constraints: Do not silently change the API contract.
tasks.hint: Move the decision logic to a function that receives actor, resource id, input, and a persistence dependency.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The service contains the business rule and exposes only explicit dependencies, making it easier to test without spinning up the HTTP layer.

modules.assessment: Demonstrate one endpoint with documented input, output, and error behavior.

modules.title: MongoDB and Mongoose Data Engineering
modules.description: Model MongoDB data around access patterns and operate it safely with schemas, validation, indexes, pagination, and consistency decisions.

lessons.title: Documents, Collections, and Modeling Choices
lessons.description: Choose embedded versus referenced data based on ownership, cardinality, and access patterns.
notes: Document modeling should follow how the application reads and writes data. Embedding is useful for bounded, tightly coupled information; references are useful when data is shared or grows independently.
lessons.summary: The intern can justify a data model in terms of application access patterns.

lessons.title: Mongoose Schemas and Validation
lessons.description: Express application invariants in Mongoose schemas without pretending schema validation replaces all application validation.
notes: Mongoose schemas can define types, defaults, enums, required fields, timestamps, and indexes. Application-level validation is still needed for request contracts and authorization.
lessons.summary: The intern can translate core data invariants into a schema.

lessons.title: CRUD, Filtering, Sorting, and Pagination
lessons.description: Implement bounded data access that avoids accidental full-collection responses.
notes: Pagination is a product and performance requirement. A server should cap client-provided limits and avoid forwarding arbitrary query keys into database filters.
lessons.summary: The API can serve large collections without accepting unbounded result sizes.

lessons.title: Indexes and Query Plans
lessons.description: Select indexes from real query patterns and verify usefulness with explain statistics.
notes: Indexes accelerate matching query shapes but add storage and write overhead. Use query plans and measured workload rather than adding indexes indiscriminately.
lessons.summary: The intern can justify an index with a query and an evidence plan.

practicals.title: Inspect a Task Query Plan
practicals.description: Create a Mongoose task schema with a query-aligned compound index and inspect the winning plan.
steps: Define Task fields and enum validation.
Add a compound index for ownerId, status, and createdAt.
Connect to MongoDB using MONGODB_URI.
Insert representative documents.
Run an owner/status query sorted by createdAt.
Inspect explain execution statistics.
practicals.output: The exercise produces actual query-plan evidence instead of assuming an index is useful merely because it exists.

lessons.title: Transactions and Consistency Boundaries
lessons.description: Recognize when multiple writes must succeed together and understand the operational cost of transactions.
notes: A transaction is useful when partial completion would violate a business invariant. It is not necessary for every CRUD request.
lessons.summary: The intern can decide whether a business operation truly requires multi-document atomicity.

tasks.title: Implement Bounded Task Pagination
tasks.description: Add filtering, pagination, and allow-listed sorting to the task endpoint.
tasks.problemStatement: GET /api/tasks must support page, limit, status, and sort without accepting arbitrary fields or unbounded limits.
constraints: Cap limit at a small server-defined maximum.
tasks.hint: Map each public sort option to a known MongoDB sort object and reject unsupported values.
tasks.solutionExplanation: Explicit allow-lists keep the public API contract narrower than the underlying database query language.

modules.assessment: Show the query shape, index choice, and explain evidence.

modules.title: Authentication and Authorization
modules.description: Implement secure account handling, authentication, token verification, role checks, and object-level authorization.

lessons.title: Authentication versus Authorization
lessons.description: Separate identity verification from permission enforcement and place both controls in server-side code.
notes: Authentication establishes who a caller is; authorization decides what that caller may do. UI controls are convenience, not a security boundary.
lessons.summary: The intern can identify whether a code path is proving identity or deciding permissions.

lessons.title: Password Storage and Registration
lessons.description: Store password verifiers using password-hashing schemes and avoid credential disclosure.
notes: Passwords should not be stored in plaintext or as reversible encryption. Use an appropriate password-hashing function and keep raw passwords out of logs, responses, and analytics.
lessons.summary: Registration produces a stored verifier, not a recoverable password.

lessons.title: JWT Bearer Authentication
lessons.description: Issue and verify short-lived access tokens and protect routes with bearer authentication.
notes: JWTs are a token format, not an authorization model by themselves. The server must still decide which resources and actions the authenticated subject may access.
lessons.summary: The intern can trace token issuance through verification to protected-route access.

practicals.title: Implement Password Hashing and Bearer Authentication
practicals.description: Implement the core authentication boundary: password hashing, verification, token issuance, and protected middleware.
steps: Hash a password with bcryptjs.
Verify a supplied password against the stored hash.
Issue a short-lived JWT containing sub and role claims.
Parse the Authorization header.
Reject missing or invalid Bearer tokens.
Keep secrets in process environment variables.
practicals.output: Registration stores only a hash; login can issue a short-lived token; protected routes require a valid Bearer credential.

lessons.title: Role and Object-Level Authorization
lessons.description: Protect privileged functions and individual resources using explicit role and ownership checks.
notes: A member may be authenticated but still forbidden from reading or modifying another member’s task. Every sensitive operation needs a server-side authorization decision.
lessons.summary: Authorization is attached to the resource/action decision, not just the login event.

lessons.title: Authentication Failure and Recovery Design
lessons.description: Review login and recovery flows for enumeration, brute-force, and unsafe recovery behavior.
notes: Authentication endpoints should avoid revealing whether an account exists. Recovery should use short-lived, single-use artifacts and never disclose the current password.
lessons.summary: The intern can review an authentication journey for information leakage and recovery weaknesses.

tasks.title: Fix a Broken Object-Level Authorization Endpoint
tasks.description: Correct an endpoint that lets an authenticated member access another member’s task.
tasks.problemStatement: The API already verifies the JWT but returns any task ID supplied by an authenticated caller. Fix the server-side authorization and add regression coverage.
constraints: Do not rely on client-side filtering.
tasks.hint: Compare the authenticated subject to the stored ownerId after locating the resource.
tasks.solutionExplanation: Authentication proves the caller is known; the owner/admin check separately establishes permission over the requested object.

modules.assessment: Demonstrate both owner success and non-owner denial.

modules.title: Frontend-Backend Integration
modules.description: Integrate the React client with the Express API using explicit contracts, authentication state, error handling, and resilient user interactions.
objectives: Represent async states and mutations clearly.

lessons.title: API Client Abstraction
lessons.description: Centralize base URL, headers, response parsing, and API errors.
learningObjectives: keep transport details out of page components
notes: A small API client reduces inconsistent headers, duplicate response parsing, and divergent error handling across components.
lessons.summary: The client has one predictable way to communicate with the API.

lessons.title: Authentication State and Browser Storage
lessons.description: Represent signed-in state deliberately and understand the security trade-offs of browser token storage.
learningObjectives: clear auth state on invalid credentials
notes: Browser storage is accessible to JavaScript running in the origin. A stronger production design often uses an HttpOnly cookie with appropriate CSRF protections; a Bearer-token exercise must document its threat model.
lessons.summary: The intern can explain why token storage is a security decision rather than a convenience setting.

lessons.title: Loading, Empty, Error, and Success States
lessons.description: Treat asynchronous UI as a state machine rather than a single “data loaded” flag.
notes: A data-driven screen may need loading, successful list, successful empty, validation failure, unauthorized, forbidden, not-found, and unexpected-error states.
lessons.summary: The UI explicitly communicates what is happening and what the user can do next.

lessons.title: Optimistic Updates and Rollback
lessons.description: Use optimistic UI only when the rollback path and failure semantics are clear.
learningObjectives: choose when pessimistic updates are better
notes: Optimistic updates can improve perceived responsiveness but create temporary client state that must reconcile with the server. They are most useful when failure is recoverable and visible.
lessons.summary: The intern can defend an optimistic UI decision in terms of consistency and rollback.

tasks.title: Integrate a Feature End-to-End
tasks.description: Add task assignment through the database, API, React UI, tests, and documentation using a feature branch.
tasks.problemStatement: Implement a task-assignment feature without breaking existing status and priority behavior.
constraints: Keep the feature small and backward compatible.
tasks.hint: Start with a written API contract and data rule, then build one vertical slice through all layers.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The feature is intentionally cross-layer so the intern must keep data model, API, authorization, UI, tests, and documentation consistent.

modules.assessment: Explain the data flow and demonstrate the feature from the browser through MongoDB.

modules.title: Testing and Debugging
modules.description: Use unit, API, integration, and browser tests to protect behavior and convert defects into durable regression coverage.
objectives: Debug from reproduction to verified fix.

lessons.title: Test Strategy and Seams
lessons.description: Choose test levels based on the risk and boundary being protected.
notes: Unit tests are fast and focused; integration tests protect boundaries between modules or infrastructure; end-to-end tests validate critical user journeys.
lessons.summary: The intern can choose a test level by considering what could realistically break.

lessons.title: Unit Testing Business Rules
lessons.description: Write deterministic tests for validation and authorization functions.
notes: Business rules such as valid priorities, permitted state transitions, or owner/admin access can often be unit-tested without a browser or live database.
lessons.summary: Focused unit tests protect rules while remaining quick to execute.

lessons.title: API and Integration Tests
lessons.description: Protect API status codes, response shapes, and authorization behavior using HTTP-level tests and an isolated test database where appropriate.
notes: API tests are valuable where bugs arise from interactions between middleware, routes, services, and persistence.
lessons.summary: The intern can write an API regression test that treats the endpoint as a contract.

lessons.title: Browser-Level Regression Testing
lessons.description: Use Playwright to protect critical user journeys without duplicating every lower-level test.
notes: Browser tests should cover high-value workflows such as login, creating a task, or completing a task rather than every possible edge case already covered at lower levels.
lessons.summary: A small number of high-value browser tests protect integration across the full UI stack.

lessons.title: Debugging and Regression Workflow
lessons.description: Turn a bug report into reproduction, root cause, fix, regression test, and verification evidence.
notes: A durable bug fix is more than changed code. The team should be able to state what failed, why, what changed, and how the test now prevents recurrence.
lessons.summary: The intern can explain a fix from symptom to verified regression coverage.

tasks.title: Write Authentication Regression Tests
tasks.description: Protect login and protected-resource behavior with integration tests.
tasks.problemStatement: Cover successful authentication, wrong credentials, missing bearer tokens, and owner/non-owner access.
constraints: Assert observable HTTP behavior, not private helper implementation.
tasks.hint: Start with the API contract and assert status code plus safe response shape.
tasks.solutionExplanation: These tests protect the authentication contract at the HTTP boundary and avoid coupling the suite to internal helper calls.

modules.assessment: Run the relevant tests and explain what failure each test would catch.

modules.title: Security, Performance, and Operations
modules.description: Apply web security guidance, dependency hygiene, performance measurement, structured logging, and release checks throughout the application.
objectives: Measure rather than guess about performance.
Prepare operationally useful logs and checks.

lessons.title: OWASP Risk Thinking for MERN
lessons.description: Map the OWASP Top 10:2025 and API Security Top 10 to concrete controls in the project.
notes: OWASP Top 10:2025 places Broken Access Control first and includes Security Misconfiguration and Software Supply Chain Failures. API Security Top 10 adds API-specific risk categories.
lessons.summary: The intern can connect risk categories to concrete code and configuration decisions.

lessons.title: Security Headers and CORS
lessons.description: Configure browser-facing protections while understanding that CORS is an origin policy mechanism, not an authentication mechanism.
notes: Helmet provides a convenient baseline for common security-related HTTP headers. CORS controls which browser origins may read responses; it does not replace server-side authorization.
lessons.summary: The intern can review browser-facing configuration without confusing it with access control.

lessons.title: Dependency and Supply-Chain Hygiene
lessons.description: Treat dependencies, lockfiles, install behavior, and release review as part of application security.
notes: OWASP Top 10:2025 treats software supply-chain failures as a distinct category. Dependency hygiene is continuous engineering work, not a one-time scan.
lessons.summary: The intern can explain why dependency choices and update workflows are security decisions.

lessons.title: Performance Measurement and Query Evidence
lessons.description: Form measurable performance questions and use database plans and browser tooling to identify bottlenecks.
notes: Performance claims require measurements. MongoDB explain execution statistics can expose examined documents and returned documents; frontend tooling can reveal network and rendering costs.
lessons.summary: The intern can connect an optimization to a measurement rather than intuition.

lessons.title: Logging, Health Checks, and Safe Diagnostics
lessons.description: Create useful operational signals without leaking secrets or excessive personal data.
notes: Logs should make failures diagnosable while remaining within data-minimization and security expectations. Health checks should report useful process/service state without exposing secrets.
lessons.summary: The application can be operated and debugged without turning logs into another data-leak channel.

practicals.title: Perform a MERN Release Security Review
practicals.description: Review a release candidate against authentication, authorization, secrets, validation, dependencies, and safe-error requirements.
steps: Inspect authentication and role checks.
Trace a protected task mutation from request to database write.
Search for hardcoded secrets and sensitive logs.
Review dependency manifests and audit output.
Inspect validation and error responses.
Write findings with evidence, remediation, owner, and verification method.
practicals.solution:
Example review checklist:
1. Authentication: protected routes reject missing/invalid credentials.
2. Authorization: task ownership or admin privilege is checked server-side.
3. Secrets: JWT_SECRET and MONGODB_URI are injected through environment configuration.
4. Validation: title, priority, and status are validated against explicit rules.
5. Errors: clients receive stable safe messages; detailed diagnostics stay server-side.
6. Dependencies: lockfiles are committed and npm audit is reviewed before release.
7. Browser controls: security headers are enabled and CORS is restricted to intended origins.
practicals.output: The deliverable is an evidence-based release review rather than a generic statement that the application is secure.

tasks.title: Perform a Release Security Review
tasks.description: Review the application against authentication, authorization, secrets, validation, dependency, and logging controls.
tasks.problemStatement: Produce a release decision backed by evidence and remediate the highest-risk issue.
constraints: Do not claim a control exists until you trace it in code/configuration.
tasks.hint: Review the request path end-to-end and verify the control where trust crosses a boundary.
tasks.solutionCode:
Release gate:
- Authentication rejects missing/invalid credentials.
- Authorization checks owner or admin before sensitive task operations.
- Secrets are not committed and are injected by environment configuration.
- Inputs are validated against explicit rules.
- Client errors do not expose stack traces.
- Dependencies are installed from the lockfile and reviewed for vulnerabilities.
- Logs do not contain passwords, access tokens, or connection strings.
tasks.solutionExplanation: A release gate is evidence-based: finding, remediation, and verification are recorded rather than replaced by a generic “secure” claim.

modules.assessment: Present findings with exact evidence and a verification method for each remediation.

modules.title: Professional Review and Release Preparation
modules.description: Practice code review, accessibility review, deployment configuration, documentation, and troubleshooting as independent engineering responsibilities.

lessons.title: Code Review as Risk Reduction
lessons.description: Review a change set for requirements, correctness, security, tests, and maintainability.
notes: A useful review comments on behavior and risk. Cosmetic preferences should not obscure defects in requirements, data handling, security, or tests.
lessons.summary: The intern can produce actionable review feedback that another developer can address.

lessons.title: Accessibility and Responsive Review
lessons.description: Inspect real pages for semantic structure, keyboard interaction, labels, focus, and responsive layout.
notes: Responsive and accessible behavior should be considered while building, then verified during review. Native HTML semantics are usually the best baseline.
lessons.summary: The intern can review UI quality as an engineering property rather than a visual preference.

lessons.title: Environment Separation and Deployment Readiness
lessons.description: Prepare environment-specific configuration without hardcoding production assumptions.
notes: A deployment plan should identify which values are configuration, which secrets require a secret manager, and which services need network access.
lessons.summary: Deployment readiness is documented even before a specific hosting provider is selected.

lessons.title: README, Runbooks, and Troubleshooting
lessons.description: Write project documentation that another developer can use to install, verify, debug, and operate the system.
notes: Good troubleshooting describes symptom, likely cause, checks, remediation, and verification.
lessons.summary: Documentation turns individual knowledge into team capability.

tasks.title: Conduct the Final Release Review
tasks.description: Review the capstone repository as a senior reviewer before release.
tasks.problemStatement: Make a release/no-release decision by checking requirements, tests, security, accessibility, configuration, and documentation.
tasks.hint: Start with acceptance criteria and trace each one to code, tests, or reproducible demonstration.
tasks.solutionCode:
Release decision checklist:
Functional: all acceptance criteria demonstrated.
Security: auth, authorization, secrets, validation, safe errors checked.
Testing: critical workflows have automated coverage.
Accessibility: labels, keyboard path, semantic structure checked.
Operations: setup, env, build, test, run commands documented.
Decision: APPROVE only when evidence supports all required categories; otherwise record blockers.
tasks.solutionExplanation: A review gate prevents “looks finished” from being mistaken for “verified.”

modules.assessment: Present blockers, evidence, and a final release recommendation.

modules.title: Final Capstone: Team Task Board
modules.description: Independently build, test, review, secure, document, and prepare a complete MERN application. This is the final practical assessment.
objectives: Translate a product brief into a backlog and architecture.
Demonstrate security, tests, accessibility, and release readiness.

lessons.title: Capstone Planning and Technical Design
lessons.description: Convert the capstone brief into milestones, data contracts, API contracts, security requirements, and a test plan.
learningObjectives: break down the work into vertical slices
notes: The final product is intentionally small enough to build but rich enough to require engineering judgment. Plan before coding, then deliver in reviewable slices.
lessons.summary: The intern starts the capstone with a plan that ties features to architecture, tests, and verification.

modules.assessment: The capstone itself is the final assessment.

project.heading: Build a Production-Style Team Task Board
project.description: Build a multi-user task management application for a small team. Members authenticate securely, create and manage owned tasks, filter their work, and update task status. Administrators receive additional management privileges. The application uses React and Vite for the client, Node.js and Express for the API, MongoDB and Mongoose for persistence, and automated tests for critical behavior. It is designed as a realistic internship capstone rather than a collection of unrelated demos.
project.problemStatement: A small delivery team needs a shared application for tracking work. Each user must be able to register or sign in, create tasks, filter them, and change status. The server must enforce ownership and administrator permissions, validate all client-controlled input, return safe errors, and persist the data reliably. The finished repository must be understandable to another developer, testable, and prepared for deployment without committing secrets.

fileWiseSolution.code:
# Team Task Board

A MERN-stack internship capstone.

## Requirements
- Current Node.js LTS compatible with the selected Vite version
- npm
- MongoDB local or reachable deployment

## Setup
1. Install root, client, and server dependencies with `npm install`.
2. Copy `.env.example` to `server/.env`.
3. Set `MONGODB_URI`, `JWT_SECRET`, `CLIENT_ORIGIN`, and `PORT`.
4. Start the API with `npm --prefix server run dev`.
5. Start the client with `npm --prefix client run dev`.

## Verification
- `GET /health` should return `{\"status\":\"ok\"}`.
- Server unit/API tests: `npm --prefix server test`.
- Client production build: `npm --prefix client run build`.
- Browser tests: `npm --prefix client run test:e2e`.

## Security
Never commit `server/.env`. Never use the sample JWT secret in production. Never log passwords, access tokens, or connection strings.

## Architecture
Browser -> React/Vite -> Express -> authentication/authorization -> Mongoose -> MongoDB -> JSON response -> React state.

## Troubleshooting
For 401 responses inspect the Bearer header and token expiry without logging the token. For MongoDB failures check `MONGODB_URI` and reachability. For client/API errors check the Vite base URL and CORS origin.

fileWiseSolution.explanation: Defines React, Vite, and browser-test tooling.
Enables the React plugin and provides a predictable local development port.
Provides the document shell and root mount point.
Mounts the application and global stylesheet.
Implements login/register, task creation, filtering, status mutation, loading/error states, and logout.
Provides responsive layout, visible focus, readable spacing, and mobile behavior.
Launches the Vite client for browser tests so test commands are reproducible.
Protects the initial accessibility contract and basic rendering of the login screen.
Declares the Express API, MongoDB/Mongoose, authentication, security, configuration, and test dependencies.
Reads environment configuration and keeps startup configuration in one place.
Defines User and Task schemas, validation, indexes, and timestamps.
Implements password hashing, verification, JWT issuance, and authentication/role middleware.
Implements authenticated task CRUD, bounded filtering, ownership authorization, and an admin user listing endpoint.
Configures security middleware, auth endpoints, task routes, health checks, and safe error handling.
Validates production configuration, connects to MongoDB, and starts the HTTP listener.
Verifies password hashing and comparison without needing a database.
Protects the operational health contract without requiring a MongoDB connection.

howItWorks.startupFlow: server.js validates required production configuration, connects to MongoDB, and starts Express. Vite serves the React application during development.
howItWorks.requestFlow: The browser sends an HTTP request. Express parses JSON, applies authentication middleware to protected routes, performs authorization checks, runs route logic, queries MongoDB through Mongoose, and returns a JSON response.
howItWorks.authenticationFlow: Register hashes the password; login verifies the hash and issues a short-lived JWT; protected routes verify the token and use its sub/role claims for authorization.
howItWorks.authorizationFlow: Task mutations load the target task, compare ownerId to the authenticated subject, and allow an administrator override.
howItWorks.testingFlow: Unit tests protect password behavior, HTTP tests protect health behavior, and Playwright protects the initial client accessibility contract. The intern is expected to add additional API and browser coverage during the internship.
howItWorks.errorFlow: Expected client errors return explicit 4xx responses; unexpected failures reach centralized middleware and become a generic 500 response.
howItWorks.deploymentFlow: Build the client with Vite, configure environment variables in the deployment platform, start the API, connect to secured MongoDB, and smoke-test health plus critical user paths.
